prompt_topic: bioresorbable vascular scaffolds in percutaneous coronary intervention
raw_text:
The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by pivotal milestones, progressing from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents, and subsequently to drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. While contemporary second-generation metallic DES have significantly improved clinical safety, they impose a permanent metal cage around the coronary vessel [2]. This permanent structure prevents physiological vasomotion, increases the risk of neoatherosclerosis, and potentially limits surgical bypass graft options in the future [3]. To overcome these challenges, bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were introduced as a transient mechanical support system that slowly degrades, ushering in the concept of "vascular restorative therapy" [4].

The earliest clinical evaluations centered on the Absorb bioresorbable everolimus-eluting scaffold (Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, CA, USA), a polymer-based scaffold constructed from a poly-L-lactide (PLLA) backbone [5]. Initial registries demonstrated successful mechanical scaffolding, low rates of target lesion revascularization, and eventual vessel restoration [6,7]. Early optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging confirmed high rates of strut coverage and scaffold resorption dynamics over two to three years [8,9].

These early successes prompted larger-scale randomized controlled trials to compare BVS with metallic DES. The ABSORB III trial demonstrated non-inferiority of the Absorb BVS compared to the metallic everolimus-eluting stent (Xience) regarding target lesion failure (TLF) at one year [10]. However, long-term safety data tempered this optimism. Extended follow-up of the ABSORB III trial and findings from the AIDA trial revealed a significantly higher risk of late scaffold thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction [11,12]. This safety concern was further confirmed by the 3-year outcomes of the ABSORB II trial [13]. Large patient-level meta-analyses and systematic reviews systematically confirmed a higher rate of both early and late scaffold thrombosis with BVS than with metallic DES [14,15,16,17].

Several factors contributed to these adverse safety signals. First-generation PLLA scaffolds had significantly thicker struts (~150 μm) compared to thin-strut metallic DES (~80 μm) [18]. This bulkier profile altered local rheology, disrupted laminar flow, and promoted platelet activation. Additionally, BVS have lower tensile strength, making them susceptible to strut fracture and malapposition if overexpanded, or incomplete lesion coverage if undersized [18,19].

To mitigate these risks, investigators standardized the "PSP" technique (Pre-dilation, Sizing, and Post-dilation) [19]. Real-world registries, such as those from Swiss, Italian, and European cohorts, demonstrated that strict adherence to the PSP protocol significantly reduced scaffold thrombosis rates [20,21,22]. Nevertheless, based on the adverse long-term clinical trial outcomes, the 2018 ESC/EACTS guidelines issued a Class III recommendation against using PLLA-based BVS in routine clinical practice [23]. Beyond stable ischemic heart disease, BVS was also explored in acute coronary syndromes, showing comparable tissue coverage but persistent safety concerns in trials such as TROFI II and other registries [24,25].

These safety concerns with polymeric scaffolds accelerated the development of alternative materials, particularly bioresorbable metallic alloys. Magnesium-based scaffolds emerged as a promising alternative due to their high radial strength, which allows for thinner struts and faster resorption times [26]. The first-generation magnesium scaffolds showed initial safety but faced limitations in radial support [27]. However, the second-generation sirolimus-eluting resorbable magnesium scaffold (Magmaris; Biotronik, Berlin, Germany) demonstrated excellent safety profiles, favorable vasomotion, and low target lesion revascularization rates in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [28,29]. These findings were subsequently confirmed in the larger BIOSOLVE-IV real-world registry, showing no definite scaffold thrombosis [30].

In conclusion, the clinical journey of BVS has transitioned from early enthusiasm to a period of caution, ultimately leading to a refinement of both technology and technique. While first-generation polymer BVS faced challenges due to thick struts, the conceptual promise of vascular restoration remains strong. Future iterations featuring ultra-thin struts, advanced magnesium or iron-based alloys, and optimized deployment techniques hold promise for the next era of percutaneous coronary intervention.
